description: For a reader about to meet an expository text whose central ideas they do not yet know, attempting a few aligned questions before reading and checking the attempts against the text afterwards is expected to improve later memory of the questioned content over reading alone, possibly at some cost to unquestioned content; one laboratory claim tests this with undergraduates, and no claim tests its classroom, comprehension or purpose-setting forms.
title: Pre-reading Questioning

description: When learners are about to study material they do not yet know, asking them to attempt questions on it first, even though most attempts will be wrong, and then letting the study, lesson or feedback supply the answers, is expected to improve later memory of the questioned content over studying for the same time without the questions; laboratory and classroom studies recorded in the wiki test this, with the gain bounded to the questioned content, dependent on the answer arriving (immediately, for arbitrary paired items) and offset in one online course by learners who stopped.
title: Pretesting (Prequestions Before Study)

description: For learners new to a system or topic whose main lesson will use many unfamiliar parts or terms, a short primer giving the name, location and behaviour of each key component before that lesson is expected to improve transfer from it over the same lesson without a primer; claims in the wiki test this (Mayer's 5 of 5 experiments, median d = 0.85, and one VR experiment), bounded by prior knowledge, the complexity and pacing of the main lesson, and short lab tests.
title: Pre-training Principle

description: For learners who must apply knowledge to ill-structured problems, organizing work around problems has a small, highly variable and possibly inflated average effect; what is better supported is guidance for novices on the target content, with a problem-first phase as a narrower option followed by instruction.
title: Problem-based Learning

description: For a novice on a procedure, a visible model, supported attempts with feedback, support withdrawn on unaided success, then mixed practice spread over sessions with the steps tied to their reasons are expected to yield accurate, fluent, retained and flexible unaided performance; no claim tests the arc as a whole, only single links in it.
title: Procedural Learning

description: Teaching writing as a staged process (plan, draft, respond, revise, edit) with feedback on drafts gives developing writers a modest gain in writing quality over product-focused teaching, tested by one meta-analysis in grades 1–12 that found no gain for struggling writers, who gain more from explicit strategy instruction.
title: Process-based Writing

description: When the goal is conceptual understanding and transfer of a new concept, having learners first attempt problems that the concept solves, before they are taught it, and then teaching it by building on their attempts, is expected to improve conceptual knowledge and transfer over teaching first, with no pooled gain on procedural skill.
title: Productive Failure

description: For adult learners, deliberate early relationship work by the instructor (learning about each learner, greeting by name, stated working terms, a brief one-to-one, low-exposure participation before public, non-punitive responses to conflict) is expected to raise willingness to participate, raise needs and engage opposing arguments, but no claim in the wiki tests this for adults: the evidence is correlational syntheses and randomised tests of single moves in middle schools.
title: Build productive instructor-learner relationships so adults feel connected and take an active role in learning

description: For learners using a simulation, practice tool or AI assistant, building the productive use into the tool (obvious productive actions, controls that invite comparison, limits on shortcuts such as answer-giving) is expected to yield more of the intended activity and better unaided performance than the same tool governed by written directions; no claim in the wiki compares the two directly, and one randomised trial shows a hints-only limit preventing harm without producing a gain.
title: Design tools so productive usage is guaranteed by affordances and constraints rather than instructions

description: For a student writer who will revise a draft, a response that names specific strengths of the text alongside a few prioritised critical comments is expected to keep the writer acting on the critique and to improve the revision, more than critique alone or generic or ability praise; no claim in the wiki tests this, and the nearest evidence (feedback meta-analyses, praise experiments with children, AI feedback audits) bounds it.
title: Provide positive comments alongside constructive criticism when responding to student writing
